Learn why partition tolerance is unavoidable in real networks
Study CP systems: choose consistency over availability during a partition
Study AP systems: choose availability over consistency during a partition
Understand eventual consistency as a practical middle ground
Learn how different databases position themselves (HBase vs Cassandra)
Explore the PACELC theorem as an extension of CAP
Apply CAP reasoning to choose a database for a specific system design scenario

name: Sharding
description: A database scaling technique that horizontally partitions data across multiple database instances called shards. Each shard holds a subset of the total data, allowing the system to handle more data and traffic than a single machine could.
roadmap: Understand the limits of vertical scaling and why sharding is needed
Learn the difference between horizontal and vertical partitioning
Study common sharding strategies: range-based, hash-based, and directory-based
Understand the challenges: cross-shard queries and hot spots
Learn about consistent hashing to minimize data movement when re-sharding
Study how MongoDB and Cassandra implement sharding
Understand the application-level complexity sharding introduces
Design a sharding strategy for a high-traffic social media feed

name: Discrete Mathematics
description: The study of mathematical structures that are fundamentally discrete rather than continuous. It covers logic, sets, relations, functions, graphs, and combinatorics — all essential to computer science theory.
roadmap: Learn propositional logic: AND, OR, NOT, implications, and truth tables
Study predicate logic and quantifiers (for all, there exists)
Understand sets, set operations, and Venn diagrams
Learn about relations, functions, and their properties
Study mathematical proofs: direct, contradiction, and induction
Explore combinatorics: permutations and combinations
Learn graph theory basics as a discrete structure
Apply discrete math concepts to algorithm analysis and CS theory

name: Linear Algebra
description: The branch of mathematics dealing with vectors, matrices, and linear transformations. It is fundamental to machine learning, computer graphics, and scientific computing.
roadmap: Understand vectors: addition, scalar multiplication, dot product
Learn matrix operations: addition, multiplication, and transpose
Study systems of linear equations and Gaussian elimination
Understand determinants and their geometric meaning
Learn about vector spaces, subspaces, and basis
Study eigenvalues and eigenvectors
Understand matrix decompositions: LU, QR, and SVD
Apply linear algebra to machine learning and PCA

name: Probability & Statistics
description: Probability models uncertainty and randomness, while statistics analyzes data to draw conclusions. Both are essential for machine learning, data science, and algorithm analysis.
roadmap: Learn basic probability: sample spaces, events, and axioms
Understand conditional probability and Bayes theorem
Study common probability distributions: uniform, binomial, Poisson, normal
Learn descriptive statistics: mean, variance, standard deviation
Understand the Central Limit Theorem and its implications
Study hypothesis testing and confidence intervals
Learn correlation, regression, and Bayesian inference basics
Apply probability and statistics to ML and algorithm analysis

name: Calculus
description: The mathematical study of continuous change through derivatives and integrals. Calculus underpins optimization algorithms like gradient descent that power machine learning.
roadmap: Review functions, limits, and continuity
Understand derivatives and rules of differentiation
Learn partial derivatives and gradients for multivariable functions
Study the chain rule as applied in neural network backpropagation
Understand integrals and the fundamental theorem of calculus
Learn optimization: finding minima and maxima using derivatives
Study Taylor series and approximations
Apply calculus concepts to gradient descent and ML optimization

name: Number Theory
description: The study of integers and their properties, including divisibility, prime numbers, and modular arithmetic. It is the mathematical foundation of modern cryptography.
roadmap: Learn divisibility, GCD, and the Euclidean algorithm
Understand prime numbers and prime factorization
Study modular arithmetic and congruences
Learn Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem
Understand the Chinese Remainder Theorem
Study RSA encryption and how it relies on number theory
Learn about discrete logarithms and their hardness
Apply number theory to cryptographic protocols

name: Graph Theory
description: The mathematical study of graphs as abstract structures representing relationships. It provides the theoretical foundation for network analysis, routing algorithms, and social network modeling.
roadmap: Understand graph definitions: vertices, edges, directed, undirected
Study graph properties: degree, paths, cycles, connectivity
Learn special graph types: trees, bipartite, planar, complete
Study graph coloring and its applications
Understand Eulerian and Hamiltonian paths and circuits
Learn about spanning trees and minimum spanning trees
Study network flows and the max-flow min-cut theorem
Apply graph theory to algorithm design and network problems

name: Set Theory
description: The branch of mathematics that studies collections of objects called sets. Set theory provides the formal language that underlies all of modern mathematics and logic.
roadmap: Understand sets: elements, membership, and notation
Learn set operations: union, intersection, difference, complement
Study Venn diagrams as a visual tool
Understand power sets and Cartesian products
Learn about relations and functions as sets
Study cardinality and infinite sets (countable vs uncountable)
Understand how set theory underpins databases and type systems
Explore Russell's paradox and axiomatic set theory basics

name: Boolean Algebra
description: An algebraic system that works with binary values (true/false or 1/0) using logical operations. It is the mathematical foundation of digital circuits and computer hardware design.
roadmap: Understand Boolean values and the three basic operations: AND, OR, NOT
Learn Boolean laws: identity, null, idempotent, complement, De Morgan's
Study truth tables for evaluating Boolean expressions
Learn how to simplify Boolean expressions using algebra
Understand Karnaugh maps for minimizing logic expressions
Study logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR) as circuit elements
Learn how Boolean algebra translates to digital circuit design
Apply Boolean logic to programming conditions and bitwise operations

name: Combinatorics
description: The branch of mathematics studying counting, arrangement, and combination of objects. Combinatorics is essential for algorithm analysis, probability, and solving enumeration problems.
roadmap: Learn the fundamental counting principle (multiplication rule)
Understand permutations: ordered arrangements of objects
Study combinations: unordered selections using binomial coefficients
Learn the Pigeonhole Principle and its applications
Study inclusion-exclusion principle for counting unions
Understand generating functions as a counting tool
Learn recurrence relations and how to solve them
Apply combinatorics to probability calculations and algorithm analysis

name: Mathematical Logic
description: The study of formal reasoning systems, including propositional and predicate logic, proof theory, and computability. It provides the theoretical underpinning of programming languages and verification.
roadmap: Study propositional logic: syntax, semantics, and connectives
Learn predicate logic: quantifiers, variables, and interpretation
Understand formal proof systems: natural deduction and sequent calculus
Study soundness and completeness of logical systems
Learn about decidability and Godel's incompleteness theorems
Understand the connection between logic and type theory
Study temporal and modal logic used in program verification
Apply mathematical logic to formal methods and compiler theory

name: Docker & Containers
description: Docker is a platform for packaging applications and their dependencies into portable containers. Containers ensure consistent environments from development through production.
roadmap: Understand what containers are and how they differ from virtual machines
Install Docker and run your first container with docker run
Learn Docker images: pulling from Docker Hub, understanding layers
Write a Dockerfile to containerize your own application
Learn essential commands: build, run, exec, logs, ps, rm
Understand Docker volumes for persistent data storage
Learn Docker networking and how containers communicate
Use Docker Compose to define and run multi-container applications

name: Kubernetes
description: An open-source system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Kubernetes is the industry standard for container orchestration at scale.
roadmap: Understand container orchestration problems that Kubernetes solves
Learn the architecture: control plane, nodes, etcd, API server
Study core objects: Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Services
Deploy an application using kubectl and YAML manifests
Understand ConfigMaps and Secrets for configuration management
Learn about namespaces, resource limits, and RBAC
Study networking: Ingress controllers and cluster DNS
Learn Helm for packaging and deploying Kubernetes applications

name: CI/CD Pipelines
description: Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment automate the process of building, testing, and deploying code changes. CI/CD pipelines reduce manual effort and catch bugs before they reach production.
roadmap: Understand the CI/CD philosophy and the problems it solves
Learn Continuous Integration: automated builds and tests on every commit
Set up a basic pipeline with GitHub Actions or GitLab CI
Understand pipeline stages: build, test, lint, security scan
Learn Continuous Deployment vs Continuous Delivery distinctions
Study deployment strategies: rolling updates, blue-green, canary
Implement environment-specific configs (dev, staging, production)
Learn about artifact management and pipeline security best practices

name: Infrastructure as Code
description: The practice of managing and provisioning infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files rather than manual processes. Terraform and Ansible are popular IaC tools.
roadmap: Understand the problems of manual infrastructure management
Learn IaC principles: declarative vs imperative approaches
Get started with Terraform: providers, resources, and state
Write Terraform configurations to provision cloud resources
Understand Terraform state management and remote backends
Learn configuration management with Ansible for server setup
Study modularity: reusable Terraform modules and Ansible roles
Apply GitOps: storing infrastructure configs in version control

name: Monitoring & Observability
description: Monitoring tracks known metrics while observability enables understanding system state from its outputs. Together they help detect, diagnose, and resolve production issues quickly.
roadmap: Understand the three pillars of observability: metrics, logs, traces
Learn about Prometheus for metrics collection and alerting
Set up Grafana dashboards to visualize metrics
Study structured logging and centralized log aggregation (ELK stack)
Understand distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry and Jaeger
Learn about SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs for reliability targets
Implement alerting rules and on-call runbooks
Study anomaly detection and capacity planning using observability data

name: Cloud Computing
description: The delivery of computing services over the internet, including servers, storage, databases, and networking. AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure dominate the cloud market.
roadmap: Understand cloud service models: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
Learn cloud deployment models: public, private, and hybrid
Get familiar with a major cloud provider (AWS, GCP, or Azure)
Study core services: compute (EC2/VMs), storage (S3/Blob), and networking
Understand cloud pricing models and cost optimization basics
Learn about managed databases, load balancers, and auto-scaling
Study Identity and Access Management (IAM) for cloud security
Build and deploy a simple application on a cloud provider

name: Linux Administration
description: Linux is the dominant operating system in server and cloud environments. System administration skills are essential for managing production infrastructure and DevOps workflows.
roadmap: Learn the Linux filesystem hierarchy and navigate with the terminal
Master essential commands: ls, cd, cp, mv, rm, chmod, chown
Understand users, groups, and file permissions
Learn process management: ps, top, kill, systemctl
Study package management with apt, yum, or dnf
Learn bash scripting for automation and task scheduling with cron
Understand networking commands: ifconfig, netstat, ssh, scp
Study log management, disk usage monitoring, and system performance tuning

name: Git & Version Control
description: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes to code over time. It enables collaboration, rollback, and branching workflows that are central to modern software development.
roadmap: Understand what version control is and why it matters
Learn the core concepts: repository, commit, branch, merge
Master essential commands: init, add, commit, status, log, diff
Understand branching and merging strategies
Learn about remote repositories and GitHub/GitLab workflows
Study pull requests, code review workflows, and collaboration patterns
Understand rebasing, cherry-picking, and conflict resolution
Learn Git best practices: commit messages, branching conventions, .gitignore

name: Serverless Architecture
description: A cloud execution model where the provider dynamically manages server allocation. Functions as a Service (FaaS) like AWS Lambda let developers deploy code without managing infrastructure.
roadmap: Understand the serverless model and its benefits over traditional servers
Learn the event-driven execution model of cloud functions
Write and deploy a basic AWS Lambda or Google Cloud Function
Understand cold starts and their performance implications
Study serverless frameworks (Serverless Framework, AWS SAM)
Learn about API Gateway for exposing functions as HTTP endpoints
Understand statelessness and how to manage state in serverless apps
Study cost model, use cases, and limitations of serverless architecture

name: Site Reliability Engineering
description: SRE applies software engineering principles to operations, treating reliability as a software problem. It was pioneered by Google and defines practices around availability, latency, and incident response.
roadmap: Understand the SRE philosophy and how it differs from traditional ops
Learn Service Level Objectives (SLOs), SLIs, and error budgets
Study on-call practices, incident response, and post-mortems
Understand toil reduction through automation
Learn capacity planning and load testing methodologies
Study chaos engineering principles for resilience testing
Understand runbooks, playbooks, and knowledge management
Read the Google SRE book and apply its principles to real systems

name: Python
description: A high-level, interpreted language known for its readable syntax and versatility. Python dominates data science, AI/ML, and scripting while being an excellent first language for beginners.
roadmap: Learn Python syntax: variables, data types, and basic I/O
Study control flow: if/else, for/while loops, and comprehensions
Understand functions, arguments, and return values
Learn Python data structures: lists, dicts, sets, and tuples
Study modules, packages, and the Python standard library
Understand object-oriented programming in Python: classes and inheritance
Learn file I/O, exception handling, and context managers
Explore popular libraries: NumPy, Pandas, Requests, and Flask

name: JavaScript
description: The programming language of the web, running natively in browsers and on servers via Node.js. JavaScript is essential for frontend development and is one of the most widely used languages in the world.
roadmap: Learn JavaScript basics: variables (let/const/var), types, and operators
Study functions: declarations, expressions, arrow functions, and scope
Understand the DOM and how JavaScript manipulates web pages
Learn arrays and objects: methods, iteration, and destructuring
Study asynchronous JavaScript: callbacks, Promises, and async/await
Understand the event loop and how JavaScript handles concurrency
Learn ES6+ features: modules, classes, spread/rest, template literals
Build projects with Node.js and explore npm ecosystem

name: TypeScript
description: A statically typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JavaScript. TypeScript adds type safety and better tooling to JavaScript, making large codebases easier to maintain.
roadmap: Understand why static typing improves large JavaScript codebases
Learn TypeScript basics: type annotations, primitives, and type inference
Study complex types: interfaces, type aliases, unions, and intersections
Understand generics for reusable, type-safe code
Learn TypeScript with classes: access modifiers, abstract classes
Study utility types: Partial, Required, Pick, Omit, Record
Configure tsconfig.json and understand compilation options
Apply TypeScript to a React or Node.js project with strict mode

name: Rust
description: A systems programming language focused on safety, speed, and concurrency. Rust prevents memory safety bugs at compile time through its unique ownership system, with no garbage collector.
roadmap: Understand Rust's goals: memory safety without GC
Learn ownership, borrowing, and the borrow checker
Study Rust types: structs, enums, and pattern matching
Understand traits as Rust's mechanism for polymorphism
Learn error handling with Result and Option types
Study lifetimes and how they express reference validity
Understand concurrency in Rust: threads, channels, and Arc/Mutex
Build a systems project: CLI tool, web server, or parser

name: Go
description: A statically typed, compiled language designed at Google for simplicity and performance. Go excels at building scalable network services and CLI tools, with built-in concurrency via goroutines.
roadmap: Learn Go syntax: variables, types, functions, and control flow
Understand Go's type system: structs, interfaces, and methods
Study error handling: returning errors as values
Learn slices, maps, and the built-in data structures
Understand goroutines for lightweight concurrency
Study channels for communication between goroutines
Learn the standard library: net/http, encoding/json, os
Build a REST API or CLI tool to solidify Go knowledge

name: C/C++
description: Low-level languages giving programmers direct control over memory and hardware. C is foundational to operating systems and embedded systems; C++ adds object-oriented features for complex applications.
roadmap: Learn C fundamentals: variables, types, control flow, and functions
Understand pointers and manual memory management (malloc/free)
Study arrays and strings as memory regions
Learn structs and how C represents compound data
Transition to C++: classes, constructors, and destructors
Understand RAII and smart pointers for safe memory management
Learn the C++ STL: vectors, maps, sets, and algorithms
Study templates, inheritance, and polymorphism in C++

name: Java
description: A widely-used, platform-independent language running on the JVM. Java is prominent in enterprise software, Android development, and large-scale backend systems with its strong OOP model.
roadmap: Learn Java basics: variables, types, operators, and control flow
Understand classes, objects, constructors, and methods
Study inheritance, interfaces, and polymorphism
Learn Java collections: ArrayList, HashMap, LinkedList
Understand exception handling with try/catch/finally
Study generics for type-safe collections and methods
Learn Java streams and functional-style programming (Java 8+)
Build a project using Maven or Gradle and explore the Java ecosystem

name: Functional Programming
description: A programming paradigm treating computation as the evaluation of mathematical functions, avoiding mutable state. FP concepts like map, filter, and immutability improve code predictability and testability.
roadmap: Understand pure functions and why they are predictable and testable
Learn about immutability and avoiding shared mutable state
Study first-class and higher-order functions
Understand map, filter, and reduce as core FP operations
Learn function composition and currying
Study recursion as the FP alternative to loops
Understand monads and functors at a conceptual level
Apply FP concepts in a language like Haskell, Elixir, or JavaScript

name: Object-Oriented Programming
description: A paradigm organizing code around objects that bundle data and behavior. OOP's four pillars — encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction — are foundational to most mainstream languages.
roadmap: Understand what objects and classes are and why they are useful
Learn encapsulation: hiding internal state with public interfaces
Study inheritance: extending classes to reuse and specialize behavior
Understand polymorphism: treating different types uniformly
Learn abstraction: hiding complexity behind simple interfaces
Study class relationships: composition vs inheritance trade-offs
Understand SOLID principles for well-designed OOP code
Apply OOP to design a real application with multiple interacting classes

name: Programming Paradigms
description: Fundamental styles of programming that shape how developers structure and reason about code. Understanding paradigms — procedural, OOP, functional, declarative — helps choose the right tool for each problem.
roadmap: Understand what a programming paradigm is and why it matters
Study imperative and procedural programming: step-by-step instructions
Learn object-oriented programming: encapsulation and objects
Understand functional programming: pure functions and immutability
Study declarative programming: describing what, not how (SQL, HTML)
Learn reactive programming: event streams and data flows
Compare multi-paradigm languages like Python, JavaScript, and Scala
Recognize which paradigm suits different problem domains

name: Design Patterns
description: Reusable solutions to commonly occurring problems in software design. The Gang of Four patterns — creational, structural, and behavioral — provide a shared vocabulary for developers.
roadmap: Understand what design patterns are and the problems they solve
Study creational patterns: Singleton, Factory, Builder, Prototype
Learn structural patterns: Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Composite
Understand behavioral patterns: Observer, Strategy, Command, Iterator
Learn to identify which pattern applies to a given problem
Study anti-patterns and how to recognize problematic designs
Apply patterns in a real codebase and evaluate trade-offs
Read the Gang of Four book or equivalent and study pattern interactions

name: Testing & QA
description: The practice of verifying software behaves correctly and meets requirements. Testing spans unit tests to end-to-end tests, and quality assurance encompasses processes that prevent defects.
roadmap: Understand the testing pyramid: unit, integration, and end-to-end tests
Write your first unit tests using a framework (Jest, PyTest, JUnit)
Learn about test coverage and what it does and does not guarantee
Understand Test-Driven Development (TDD): red-green-refactor cycle
Study mocking and stubbing to isolate units under test
Learn integration testing strategies for testing component interactions
Understand end-to-end testing tools (Playwright, Cypress)
Study CI integration: running tests automatically on every commit

name: Agile & Scrum
description: Agile is a mindset for iterative, customer-focused software development. Scrum is the most popular Agile framework, using time-boxed sprints and defined ceremonies to manage work.
roadmap: Read the Agile Manifesto and understand its four values and twelve principles
Learn the Scrum framework: roles, events, and artifacts
Understand sprints: planning, daily standups, review, and retrospective
Learn about the Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and user stories
Study estimation techniques: story points and planning poker
Understand Kanban as an alternative to Scrum
Learn common Agile metrics: velocity, burndown, cycle time
Apply Agile practices in a team setting and reflect on what works

name: System Design
description: The process of defining architecture, components, and data flows for large-scale systems. System design is tested in senior engineering interviews and is essential for building reliable, scalable products.
roadmap: Learn to clarify requirements: functional, non-functional, and constraints
Study capacity estimation: users, QPS, storage, and bandwidth
Understand horizontal vs vertical scaling trade-offs
Learn load balancing strategies and consistent hashing
Study caching layers: CDN, application cache, database cache
Understand database choices: SQL vs NoSQL, sharding, replication
Learn asynchronous processing with message queues (Kafka, RabbitMQ)
Practice designing real systems: URL shortener, Twitter feed, Netflix

name: Code Review
description: The systematic examination of source code by peers to find bugs, improve quality, and share knowledge. Effective code review is one of the highest-ROI practices in software engineering.
roadmap: Understand the goals of code review: correctness, readability, knowledge sharing
Learn what to look for: logic errors, security issues, performance, style
Study how to give constructive, actionable feedback
Understand how to receive feedback professionally
Learn the difference between blocking and non-blocking comments
Study automated tools (linters, static analyzers) that complement review
Understand review conventions: PR size, description quality, and response time
Develop a team code review culture and process guidelines

name: Technical Debt
description: The implied cost of future rework caused by choosing quick, easy solutions now over better approaches. Managing technical debt is crucial for maintaining long-term development velocity.
roadmap: Understand what technical debt is and Ward Cunningham's original metaphor
Learn to distinguish intentional (strategic) from accidental debt
Study how debt accumulates and compounds over time
Learn to identify debt: code smells, missing tests, outdated dependencies
Understand how to measure and communicate debt to stakeholders
Study refactoring techniques for safely paying down debt
Learn to balance new feature development with debt reduction
Develop strategies for preventing excessive debt accumulation

name: API Design
description: The practice of designing interfaces that allow software components to communicate. Good API design prioritizes clarity, consistency, and evolvability, making integrations easier and more reliable.
roadmap: Understand what an API is and why good design matters
Study REST principles: resources, HTTP methods, and status codes
Learn URL naming conventions and resource hierarchy design
Understand request/response formats and JSON API standards
Study versioning strategies: URL versioning vs header versioning
Learn authentication and authorization in APIs (OAuth, API keys)
Understand error handling: consistent error formats and meaningful messages
Document your API with OpenAPI/Swagger and maintain it as you evolve

name: Microservices Architecture
description: An architectural style structuring an application as a collection of small, independently deployable services. Each service owns its data and communicates over APIs, enabling team autonomy and scalability.
roadmap: Understand monoliths vs microservices: trade-offs and when to split
Learn service decomposition strategies based on domain boundaries (DDD)
Study inter-service communication: synchronous REST/gRPC vs async messaging
Understand data management: each service owns its data (database per service)
Learn service discovery, API gateways, and load balancing
Study distributed systems challenges: eventual consistency and sagas
Understand observability in microservices: distributed tracing
Learn deployment patterns: sidecar, service mesh, and container orchestration

name: Clean Code Principles
description: A set of practices that make code readable, maintainable, and understandable. Clean code is not just about style — it is about writing code that future developers (including yourself) can work with confidently.
roadmap: Understand why code is read far more often than it is written
Learn meaningful naming: variables, functions, and classes that reveal intent
Study the Single Responsibility Principle for functions and classes
Understand small, focused functions and the principle of doing one thing
Learn to eliminate comments by writing self-documenting code
Study DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) and how to remove duplication
Understand error handling: use exceptions meaningfully
Read Clean Code by Robert Martin and apply principles through practice

name: Software Architecture
description: The high-level structure of a software system, defining how components are organized and interact. Good architecture enables a system to meet both functional requirements and quality attributes like scalability and maintainability.
roadmap: Understand what architecture is and why it matters for long-term systems
Study common architectural patterns: layered, event-driven, hexagonal
Learn Domain-Driven Design (DDD) and bounded contexts
Understand the CAP theorem and its implications for distributed systems
Study CQRS and Event Sourcing patterns
Learn to document architecture with C4 diagrams
Understand architectural decision records (ADRs) for capturing decisions
Evaluate architectural trade-offs against quality attributes (NFRs)

name: Topological Sort
description: An ordering of vertices in a directed acyclic graph such that every edge points from an earlier vertex to a later one. It is used for dependency resolution, task scheduling, and build systems.
roadmap: Understand directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and their properties
Learn why topological ordering exists only for DAGs
Implement topological sort using DFS with a completion stack
Implement Kahn's algorithm using in-degree and BFS
Understand cycle detection as part of topological sort
Apply to build system dependency resolution problems
Practice on course prerequisite and task scheduling problems

name: Floyd-Warshall
description: A dynamic programming algorithm for finding shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in a weighted graph. It handles negative edge weights and runs in O(n³) time.
roadmap: Understand the all-pairs shortest path problem
Review single-source shortest path as motivation
Learn the Floyd-Warshall recurrence: dp[i][j][k]
Implement the algorithm and trace through a small example
Understand how to detect negative cycles using the diagonal
Compare to running Dijkstra from every vertex
Apply to network routing and transitive closure problems

name: Bellman-Ford
description: A single-source shortest path algorithm that handles graphs with negative edge weights. Unlike Dijkstra, it can detect negative weight cycles and runs in O(VE) time.
roadmap: Understand why Dijkstra fails on negative weight edges
Learn the Bellman-Ford relaxation approach
Implement the algorithm: relax all edges V-1 times
Understand negative cycle detection on the Vth iteration
Compare Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra: when to use each
Apply to currency arbitrage detection as a classic use case
Practice on competitive programming shortest path problems

name: Bit Manipulation
description: Techniques for directly operating on individual bits within integers using bitwise operators. Bit manipulation enables highly efficient algorithms for problems involving flags, sets, and arithmetic.
roadmap: Understand binary representation of integers
Learn bitwise operators: AND, OR, XOR, NOT, left shift, right shift
Master common tricks: check/set/clear/toggle a bit
Understand two's complement and signed integers
Learn XOR tricks: find the unique element, swap without temp
Study bit masking for working with subsets
Practice bit manipulation problems on LeetCode
Apply to competitive programming and low-level optimization

name: Sliding Window
description: A technique for solving problems on arrays or strings by maintaining a window that moves across the data. It reduces O(n²) brute-force solutions to O(n) by avoiding redundant computation.
roadmap: Understand the two-pointer technique as a foundation
Learn the fixed-size window pattern with examples
Study the variable-size window with two-pointer shrink/expand
Implement maximum sum subarray of size k
Solve longest substring without repeating characters
Study the minimum window substring problem
Learn when sliding window applies: contiguous subarrays/substrings
Practice sliding window problems across LeetCode patterns

name: Segment Trees
description: A tree data structure for storing intervals or segments, enabling efficient range queries and point updates. Segment trees answer range sum/min/max queries in O(log n) time.
roadmap: Understand the range query problem and naive O(n) approach
Learn the segment tree structure and how it stores intervals
Implement build, query, and update operations recursively
Understand lazy propagation for efficient range updates
Study the iterative (bottom-up) segment tree implementation
Learn persistent segment trees for historical queries
Apply to range sum, range min, and range max problems
Practice segment tree problems on Codeforces and LeetCode

name: Disjoint Sets
description: Also called Union-Find, this data structure tracks a set of elements partitioned into disjoint subsets. With union by rank and path compression, operations run in nearly O(1) amortized time.
roadmap: Understand the problem: tracking connected components dynamically
Implement naive union-find with arrays
Learn union by rank to keep trees shallow
Implement path compression for nearly O(1) find
Prove the amortized complexity with both optimizations
Apply to Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm
Use Union-Find to detect cycles in undirected graphs
Solve connected components and percolation problems

name: Deques
description: A double-ended queue that supports efficient insertion and deletion at both front and back. Deques are used in sliding window algorithms, palindrome checking, and work-stealing schedulers.
roadmap: Understand the deque as a generalization of stack and queue
Learn operations: push_front, push_back, pop_front, pop_back
Implement a deque using a doubly linked list
Implement a deque using a circular buffer for O(1) operations
Study the sliding window maximum problem using a monotonic deque
Understand Python's collections.deque and Java's ArrayDeque
Apply deques to BFS with priority and scheduling problems

name: Circular Buffers
description: A fixed-size buffer that wraps around to the beginning when it reaches the end, acting as if the memory is circular. Circular buffers are widely used in streaming, audio processing, and producer-consumer scenarios.
roadmap: Understand the fixed-size buffer problem and why wrapping helps
Learn the head and tail pointer approach
Implement a circular buffer with enqueue and dequeue
Handle the full/empty distinction (use size counter or sentinel)
Understand lock-free circular buffers for concurrent use
Study applications in audio streaming, logging, and networking
Compare to dynamic arrays and linked list queues

name: Adjacency Lists
description: A way to represent graphs where each vertex stores a list of its neighbors. Adjacency lists are memory-efficient for sparse graphs and are the standard representation for most graph algorithms.
roadmap: Understand the two main graph representations: matrix vs list
Learn why adjacency lists are better for sparse graphs
Implement an adjacency list using arrays of lists
Implement a weighted graph with edge weights stored in the list
Understand directed vs undirected representation differences
Study time/space complexity: O(V+E) space, O(degree) iteration
Use adjacency lists to implement BFS and DFS
Contrast with adjacency matrices for dense graph use cases

name: Containerization
description: A lightweight virtualization method that packages an application with its dependencies into a self-contained unit. Containers share the host OS kernel, making them faster and more resource-efficient than VMs.
roadmap: Understand the difference between containers and virtual machines
Learn Linux primitives: namespaces for isolation and cgroups for resources
Understand how Docker uses these primitives to create containers
Study container images: layers, copy-on-write filesystems
Learn container networking: bridge networks, host networking, overlay
Understand container storage: bind mounts and volumes
Study container security: reducing attack surface and privilege escalation
Understand container runtimes: OCI spec, containerd, and Docker

name: Kernel
description: The core component of an operating system that manages hardware resources and provides services to user processes. The kernel mediates access to CPU, memory, devices, and the file system.
roadmap: Understand the kernel's role in an operating system
Learn the distinction between kernel space and user space
Study monolithic kernels vs microkernels trade-offs
Understand the Linux kernel architecture and major subsystems
Learn how system calls cross the user/kernel boundary
Study the kernel scheduler and how it manages CPU time
Understand memory management: virtual memory and the page allocator
Explore kernel modules and device drivers as extension mechanisms

name: System Calls
description: The interface through which user-space programs request services from the operating system kernel. System calls provide controlled access to privileged operations like file I/O, process creation, and networking.
roadmap: Understand the user-space/kernel-space boundary and why it exists
Learn how a system call transitions from user mode to kernel mode
Study common POSIX system calls: read, write, open, fork, exec, wait
Understand file descriptors and the Unix I/O model
Learn process management syscalls: fork, exec, wait, kill, signal
Study the overhead of system calls and why they should be batched
Use strace to observe system calls made by real programs
Understand how libc wraps system calls into portable interfaces

name: Inter-Process Communication
description: Mechanisms that allow processes to exchange data and synchronize with each other. IPC includes pipes, message queues, shared memory, and sockets, each with different performance and complexity trade-offs.
roadmap: Understand why processes need to communicate and the isolation barrier
Learn about pipes: anonymous pipes for parent-child and named pipes (FIFOs)
Study message queues for asynchronous process communication
Understand shared memory as the fastest IPC mechanism
Learn semaphores and mutexes for synchronizing shared memory access
Study Unix domain sockets for local high-performance IPC
Understand signals as asynchronous notifications between processes
Compare IPC mechanisms by performance, complexity, and use case

name: Caching Strategies
description: Techniques for storing copies of data in faster storage to reduce latency and load. Caching is foundational to performance in CPUs, databases, web applications, and distributed systems.
roadmap: Understand the cache hierarchy: L1/L2/L3 CPU caches, RAM, disk
Learn cache hit/miss and the principle of locality
Study eviction policies: LRU, LFU, FIFO, and random
Implement an LRU cache using a hash map and doubly linked list
Learn write policies: write-through vs write-back vs write-around
Study cache invalidation strategies and cache coherence
Understand distributed caching with Redis and Memcached
Learn CDN caching and HTTP cache control headers

name: Progressive Web Apps
description: Web applications that use modern APIs to deliver app-like experiences with offline support, push notifications, and installability. PWAs bridge the gap between web and native apps.
roadmap: Understand what makes a web app progressive and the PWA checklist
Learn about HTTPS as a PWA requirement
Study Web App Manifests for installability and splash screens
Understand Service Workers: lifecycle, registration, and events
Implement offline caching strategies with the Cache API
Learn background sync for deferred actions
Study push notifications using the Push and Notifications APIs
Audit a PWA with Lighthouse and achieve a high PWA score

name: Server Components
description: A React paradigm where components render on the server, sending only HTML to the client with zero JavaScript overhead. Server Components reduce bundle size and enable direct database access from components.
roadmap: Understand the distinction between Server and Client Components
Learn why Server Components have zero bundle size impact
Study the React Server Component rendering model
Understand the rules: no hooks, no browser APIs in Server Components
Learn data fetching patterns directly in Server Components
Understand streaming and Suspense integration
Study when to use Client Components vs Server Components
Build a Next.js App Router application using Server Components effectively

name: Edge Computing
description: Processing data closer to the user at the network edge rather than in a centralized data center. Edge computing reduces latency for web applications by running code geographically near the end user.
roadmap: Understand the latency problem that edge computing solves
Learn about CDN edge networks and how they work
Study edge runtimes: Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge, Deno Deploy
Understand the V8 isolates model used at the edge
Learn constraints of edge environments: no Node.js APIs, limited compute
Study use cases: personalization, A/B testing, auth at the edge
Implement a simple edge function and measure latency improvements
Understand edge databases (D1, Turso) for data at the edge

name: Web Workers
description: A browser API for running JavaScript in background threads, separate from the main UI thread. Web Workers prevent heavy computation from blocking the browser and causing unresponsive interfaces.
roadmap: Understand the single-threaded browser model and why it causes jank
Learn the Web Worker API: creating and terminating workers
Study message passing between the main thread and workers
Understand what workers cannot access: DOM, window object
Learn SharedArrayBuffer for shared memory between threads
Study Atomics for synchronizing shared memory access
Understand Comlink for ergonomic worker communication
Apply workers to heavy computation: image processing, parsing, crypto

name: WebAssembly
description: A binary instruction format that runs in browsers at near-native speed. WebAssembly allows languages like C, C++, and Rust to run on the web, enabling performance-critical applications in the browser.
roadmap: Understand what WebAssembly is and the problems it solves
Learn the WebAssembly text format (WAT) and binary format
Understand the WebAssembly execution model and memory model
Compile a simple C or Rust program to WebAssembly
Learn the JavaScript API for loading and running WASM modules
Study Emscripten for compiling C/C++ projects to WebAssembly
Understand WASI for running WebAssembly outside the browser
Build a performance-critical application using WASM

name: QUIC Protocol
description: A modern transport protocol built on UDP that provides HTTP/3's foundation. QUIC reduces latency through 0-RTT connections, improved loss recovery, and eliminating head-of-line blocking.
roadmap: Understand the limitations of TCP that motivated QUIC
Learn how QUIC is built on UDP and why
Study QUIC's connection establishment and 0-RTT resumption
Understand stream multiplexing and how QUIC eliminates head-of-line blocking
Learn QUIC's built-in TLS 1.3 integration
Study connection migration and how QUIC handles IP changes
Understand HTTP/3 as the HTTP mapping over QUIC
Analyze QUIC performance improvements over TCP with real measurements

name: Network Address Translation
description: A method of remapping IP addresses as traffic passes through a router, allowing multiple devices to share a single public IP. NAT is ubiquitous in home and enterprise networks.
roadmap: Understand IPv4 address exhaustion and the problem NAT solves
Learn the difference between public and private IP address ranges
Understand how NAT tracks connections using a translation table
Study SNAT (source NAT) and DNAT (destination NAT)
Learn about PAT (Port Address Translation) / IP masquerading
Understand NAT traversal challenges for peer-to-peer applications
Study NAT hole-punching techniques used by WebRTC and VoIP
Understand how IPv6 aims to eliminate the need for NAT

name: Software Defined Networking
description: An approach to networking that separates the control plane from the data plane, centralizing network intelligence in software. SDN enables programmable, flexible network management at scale.
roadmap: Understand traditional networking: tightly coupled control and data planes
Learn the SDN architecture: controller, southbound API, data plane
Study OpenFlow as the original SDN protocol
Understand the SDN controller: logical centralization of network state
Learn network virtualization and virtual overlays (VXLAN)
Study SDN use cases: data center networking, WAN optimization
Understand NFV (Network Function Virtualization) and its relation to SDN
Explore open-source SDN controllers like OpenDaylight and ONOS

name: MQTT
description: A lightweight publish-subscribe messaging protocol designed for constrained devices and low-bandwidth networks. MQTT is the dominant protocol for IoT applications and machine-to-machine communication.
roadmap: Understand the publish-subscribe pattern and its advantages
Learn MQTT's design goals: lightweight, low-bandwidth, IoT-focused
Study MQTT architecture: broker, publishers, and subscribers
Learn about topics and topic hierarchy for message routing
Understand QoS levels: at most once, at least once, exactly once
Study the Last Will and Testament for detecting client disconnects
Set up a Mosquitto MQTT broker and build a simple pub-sub system
Apply MQTT to an IoT project with sensor data streaming

name: WebRTC
description: A browser API and protocol suite enabling real-time peer-to-peer audio, video, and data communication. WebRTC powers video conferencing, screen sharing, and live streaming directly in the browser.
roadmap: Understand what WebRTC is and the problems it solves
Learn the WebRTC API: RTCPeerConnection, getUserMedia, RTCDataChannel
Understand the signaling process and why WebRTC needs an external signaling server
Study ICE, STUN, and TURN for NAT traversal
Learn the SDP offer/answer model for capability negotiation
Understand SRTP and DTLS for encrypted media transport
Build a simple video call application using WebRTC
Study scalable architectures: SFU vs MCU for multi-party calls

name: Zero Trust Architecture
description: A security model that eliminates implicit trust based on network location, requiring verification for every request. Zero trust treats every access attempt as potentially hostile regardless of origin.
roadmap: Understand the failure of perimeter-based security models
Learn the zero trust principle: never trust, always verify
Study the three core concepts: identity, device, and least privilege
Understand identity-centric security and strong authentication (MFA)
Learn micro-segmentation for limiting lateral movement
Study continuous monitoring and dynamic policy enforcement
Understand BeyondCorp (Google's zero trust implementation) as a case study
Plan a zero trust implementation roadmap for an organization

name: Security Operations Center
description: A SOC is a team and facility centralized to monitor, detect, and respond to security threats. SOC operations combine people, processes, and technology to defend organizations continuously.
roadmap: Understand the SOC mission: monitor, detect, respond
Learn SOC tiers: L1 analyst to L3 threat hunter roles
Study SIEM platforms for log aggregation and correlation (Splunk, Elastic)
Understand the incident response lifecycle: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate
Learn about threat intelligence feeds and IOCs
Study playbooks and runbooks for standardized response
Understand SOAR platforms for automating incident response
Learn metrics: MTTD (mean time to detect) and MTTR (mean time to respond)

name: Threat Modeling
description: A structured process for identifying, prioritizing, and mitigating security threats during system design. Threat modeling shifts security left by catching vulnerabilities before they are built.
roadmap: Understand why designing security in is cheaper than retrofitting
Learn the four-question threat modeling framework
Study data flow diagrams (DFDs) for visualizing system components
Learn STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info disclosure, DoS, Elevation
Understand DREAD and CVSS for risk scoring
Practice threat modeling on a simple web application architecture
Learn attack trees as a complementary analysis technique
Integrate threat modeling into the SDLC and design review process

name: Bug Bounty Programs
description: Programs where organizations reward security researchers for responsibly disclosing vulnerabilities. Bug bounties create incentives for ethical hacking and have become standard practice at major tech companies.
roadmap: Understand the responsible disclosure model and its benefits
Learn how bug bounty programs are structured (scope, payouts, rules)
Study platforms: HackerOne, Bugcrowd, and Intigriti
Learn common vulnerability classes: XSS, CSRF, SSRF, IDOR, SQLi
Study the OWASP Top 10 as a starting point for vulnerability research
Set up a local lab environment for safe practice (DVWA, HackTheBox)
Understand report writing: clear reproduction steps and impact analysis
Begin with programs labeled beginner-friendly and build up experience

name: Supply Chain Security
description: Protecting software and its dependencies from compromised components introduced during development or delivery. Supply chain attacks like SolarWinds and Log4Shell highlight this growing threat vector.
roadmap: Understand software supply chain attacks and notable incidents
Learn about dependency confusion and typosquatting attacks
Study Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for dependency visibility
Understand package signing and verification (Sigstore, GPG)
Learn about vulnerability scanning for dependencies (Dependabot, Snyk)
Study secure build pipelines and reproducible builds
Understand SLSA framework levels for supply chain integrity
Implement dependency pinning and automated security updates

name: Time Series Databases
description: Databases optimized for storing and querying data points indexed by time. They excel at metrics, monitoring, IoT sensor data, and financial data with specialized compression and query capabilities.
roadmap: Understand what makes time series data unique: append-heavy, time-ordered
Learn why general-purpose databases struggle with time series workloads
Study time series database architecture and columnar storage
Get started with InfluxDB or TimescaleDB
Learn the time series data model: measurements, tags, fields
Understand downsampling and retention policies for data lifecycle
Study time-based queries: range queries, aggregations, sliding windows
Apply to a monitoring or IoT project with real metrics

name: Graph Databases
description: Databases that store data as nodes and edges, optimized for querying highly connected data. Graph databases excel at social networks, recommendation engines, and fraud detection.
roadmap: Understand the property graph model: nodes, edges, and properties
Learn why relational databases struggle with highly connected data
Get started with Neo4j and the Cypher query language
Study graph traversal queries: finding paths and neighbors
Understand graph algorithms in databases: PageRank, shortest path
Learn about RDF and SPARQL as the semantic web alternative
Study use cases: social networks, knowledge graphs, fraud detection
Design a graph data model for a real application

name: Database Migration
description: The process of managing incremental, versioned changes to a database schema over time. Migration tools like Flyway and Alembic enable safe, repeatable schema evolution in team environments.
roadmap: Understand why schema changes must be managed carefully in production
Learn the migration file pattern: sequential, versioned SQL scripts
Set up a migration tool: Flyway (Java), Alembic (Python), or Knex (JS)
Understand the up/down migration pattern for reversibility
Study zero-downtime migration techniques: expand-contract pattern
Learn about backward-compatible schema changes for safe deployments
Understand migration in CI/CD: automating migrations in deployment pipelines
Handle data migrations: transforming existing data safely

name: Connection Pooling
description: A technique for reusing database connections rather than opening a new one for each request. Connection pooling dramatically reduces overhead and improves throughput for database-heavy applications.
roadmap: Understand the cost of establishing a new database connection
Learn what a connection pool is and how it maintains warm connections
Study pool configuration: min/max pool size and connection timeout
Understand connection lifecycle: acquire, use, release, eviction
Learn about connection pool exhaustion and how to diagnose it
Study tools: pgBouncer for PostgreSQL, HikariCP for Java
Understand the difference between client-side and server-side pooling
Configure connection pooling for a production application

name: Write-Ahead Logging
description: A technique where changes are logged to a sequential log before being applied to the database, ensuring durability and enabling recovery after crashes. WAL is the backbone of ACID compliance in most databases.
roadmap: Understand the durability challenge: ensuring committed data survives crashes
Learn the WAL principle: log before apply
Study the WAL structure: log sequence numbers and log records
Understand ARIES recovery algorithm: analysis, redo, undo phases
Learn how PostgreSQL uses WAL for crash recovery
Understand WAL-based replication for high availability
Study logical decoding and WAL as a change data capture (CDC) source
Analyze WAL performance trade-offs: fsync, checkpoints, and write amplification
